title: What are @QueryHints in JPA, what hints like readOnly, cacheable, fetchSize, and timeout control, and how do method-level and transaction-level settings differ?
keyPoints: @QueryHints attaches JPA/Hibernate hints to a single repository method, tuning that specific query without affecting others.
The readOnly hint loads entities without dirty-check snapshots, roughly halving their memory footprint.
The cacheable hint routes a query through Hibernate's query cache, ideal for rarely-changing lookups like branch codes.
The fetchSize hint controls how many rows the JDBC driver pulls per round trip, essential for streaming large result sets.
The query timeout hint aborts a slow query after N milliseconds, protecting the system from pool exhaustion.
Method-level hints affect one query; @Transactional(readOnly=true) affects the whole transaction including JDBC connection routing.

s1_definition.oneliner: @QueryHints fine-tune a single query (readOnly, cacheable, fetchSize, timeout); @Transactional(readOnly) sets the policy for the whole transaction.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **@QueryHints** – attaches JPA or Hibernate query hints to a specific repository method, tuning that query's execution without changing what it returns.
- **org.hibernate.readOnly** – loads entities without dirty-check snapshots, saving memory and guaranteeing no accidental flush.
- **org.hibernate.cacheable** – routes the query through Hibernate's query cache so repeated identical queries return cached results.
- **org.hibernate.fetchSize** – sets the JDBC fetch size, controlling how many rows the driver pulls per round trip from the database.
- **jakarta.persistence.query.timeout** – aborts a query that runs longer than N milliseconds, protecting the system from runaway reports.
- **Method vs transaction level** – a query hint affects one query; @Transactional(readOnly=true) affects every query in the transaction and sets the JDBC connection read-only.
s1_definition.analogy: Query hints are special instructions National Bank of India pins to a single request slip. The readOnly note tells the clerk not to bother snapshotting for changes. The cacheable note says if you fetched this exact list recently, reuse it. The fetchSize note says bring records in bundles of a thousand instead of all at once. The timeout note says if this takes longer than three seconds, give up. Pinning the note to one slip (method level) affects just that request; posting it on the department door (transaction level) affects everything during the whole visit.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  @QueryHints vs @Transactional Scope
  ============================================

  @Transactional(readOnly=true, timeout=30)
  +-------------------------------------------------------+
  |  ALL queries in this transaction:                      |
  |  - JDBC connection = read-only                         |
  |  - FlushMode = MANUAL (no dirty check for ANY entity)  |
  |  - TX timeout = 30 seconds total                       |
  |                                                        |
  |  @QueryHints(readOnly, timeout=3000)                   |
  |  +------------------------------------------+          |
  |  | THIS query only:                         |          |
  |  | - Entities loaded without snapshot        |          |
  |  | - Query aborts after 3 seconds            |          |
  |  +------------------------------------------+          |
  |                                                        |
  |  Other queries in same TX:                             |
  |  - Use TX-level settings (readOnly, 30s timeout)       |
  |  - NOT affected by method-level hints                  |
  +-------------------------------------------------------+

  fetchSize Streaming Flow
  ============================================
  Driver fetches rows in chunks:

  Application          JDBC Driver          Database
      |                    |                    |
      |--- next() -------->|                    |
      |                    |--- FETCH 1000 ---->|
      |<-- 1000 rows ------|<-- 1000 rows ------||
      |--- process ------->|                    |
      |--- next() -------->|                    |
      |                    |--- FETCH 1000 ---->|
      |<-- 1000 rows ------|<-- 1000 rows ------|
      |    (memory flat)   |                    |
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Query hints let Rajesh tune an individual query's execution at National Bank of India without changing what it returns. The readOnly hint loads entities without dirty-check snapshots, roughly halving their memory footprint and guaranteeing they are never flushed as updates. The cacheable hint routes a query through Hibernate's query cache, ideal for the branch-code lookup that is read constantly and almost never changes. The fetchSize hint controls how many rows the JDBC driver pulls per round trip, essential for the regulatory export that streams millions of transactions without blowing up the heap. The query timeout hint aborts a slow query, protecting the system from a runaway search exhausting the connection pool.

The method-level versus transaction-level distinction matters. A query hint affects exactly one query, while @Transactional(readOnly=true) affects every query in the transaction and additionally sets the JDBC connection read-only for replica routing. They compose cleanly: Rajesh can run a writable transaction overall yet mark one expensive reporting query read-only through a hint, and he can bound a single query with a 3-second timeout while bounding the whole transaction with a 30-second timeout.

The senior cautions Pankaj gives are that the query cache only pays off when the data is genuinely read-mostly, that fetchSize behaviour is driver-specific and PostgreSQL needs autocommit off to honour it, and that a query timeout on every customer-facing endpoint is not optional because one slow wildcard search without a timeout can cascade into a pool exhaustion outage.

Remember one sentence: @QueryHints tunes one query with readOnly, cacheable, fetchSize, or timeout, while @Transactional sets the policy for the whole transaction.
